notes.meaning: God now turns to Moab, a nation east of the Dead Sea. The words "three sins, even four" mean sin piled on sin, until God would no longer hold back. Moab's crime was cruelty: they burned the bones of Edom's king until they were like powdered lime. Digging up or burning a dead body showed a savage, hateful spirit, even against a related people.

The "fire" stands for war that would burn Moab's strong buildings. Kerioth was one of Moab's main cities. Moab would fall in the noise of battle, with shouting and the blast of the ram's horn, the war trumpet. Those who deal cruelly will be cruelly dealt with.

The "ruler" (literally "judge") likely means the king, the chief ruler of Moab. He and all his officials would be killed. The ruler who ordered the bones burned would learn there is a higher Judge. Without leaders, Moab would cease to be a nation.

Now God speaks to Judah, His own people, using the same words He used for the pagan nations. The other nations were judged for harming people, but Judah was judged for dishonoring God. They rejected His law, the teaching He gave through Moses. The "lies" are idols, false gods that fool those who trust them. Following what their fathers did was no excuse.

differ.view: Calvin reads the "lies" as ways of worship people invent for themselves and defend as well meant; any step away from God's word leads into more error.

notes.meaning: Even Jerusalem, the holy city, would be burned. This came true when the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem. Being God's chosen people did not protect Judah from punishment.

At last Amos reaches his real target: Israel, the northern kingdom. Their judges took bribes to condemn innocent people. They would sell out a poor man for something as small as a pair of sandals. Once people sell their conscience for silver, they soon sell it for almost nothing.

The rich were greedy to crush the poor, pressing them down until they sat in the dust like mourners. They pushed gentle, helpless people out of the way and blocked their path to justice. A father and son slept with the same young woman, a sin close to incest. Such behavior by people who claimed God's name brought shame on that holy name.

God's law said a poor man's cloak taken as a pledge for a loan had to be returned by sunset, since it was his blanket. These lenders kept the cloaks and lounged on them at feasts beside the altars. They drank wine bought with unfair fines in the house of their God. They thought religious ceremonies would cover their greed, as if God would share in their stolen goods.

God reminds Israel of what He had done for them. The Amorites, standing for all the peoples of Canaan, were huge and strong like cedars and oaks. Israel could never have beaten them alone, but God destroyed them completely, "root and branch." Remembering this mercy makes Israel's ungratefulness even worse.

God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt. He led and fed them for forty years in the wilderness. Then He gave them the land of the Amorites. These years also trained a crowd of wanderers to become a nation that lived by His ways.

God also gave Israel spiritual gifts. He raised up prophets from their own families to speak His word. He raised up Nazirites, young people who made a vow to God and gave up wine, as living examples of holy living. God asks, "Is this not true?" so that their own hearts would admit it.

Israel fought against these gifts. They coaxed or pressured the Nazirites into drinking wine and breaking their vow. They ordered the prophets to stop speaking, just as a priest later told Amos to go away (Amos 7:12). They wanted preachers who would flatter them, not warn them.

The picture is of a farm cart loaded heavy with harvest grain. Older translations read it as God saying He is weighed down by Israel's sins, like an overloaded cart. Others, like the BSB, read it as God pressing Israel down under His judgment, like a heavy cart crushing the ground. Either way, Israel's sin will bring heavy judgment.

When the invading army comes, no one will escape. The fast runner, the strong man, the archer, and the horseman will all fail. Even the bravest soldier will throw off his clothes and weapons and run for his life. When God judges, no human strength or skill can save.
